A_general.open_code_note: The public repository is Close’s Cursor plugin: configuration, workflows, and a skill that connect directly to the hosted endpoint. It does not implement the MCP server.
A_general.implementation_language: NOT FOUND for server; plugin contains Markdown, JSON, and JavaScript
A_general.mcp_sdk_and_version: NOT FOUND; the public plugin repository has no MCP server SDK dependency
other_official_servers: https://help.close.com/_mcp/server — the Help Center documentation’s own AI client/search endpoint; distinct from the Close CRM server.

B_access_pricing.mcp_access_cost_details: No MCP-specific charge or limit was found. Access requires connection to a Close organization and authorization; the documentation does not state whether MCP access requires a particular subscription plan.
B_access_pricing.linked_software_cost: Close lists Solo at $19/user/month or $9/user/month with annual billing; Essentials $49 or $35; Growth $109 or $99; Scale $149 or $139. The page also offers a free trial.
B_access_pricing.pricing_model_details: Listed plans are priced per user per month. Close separately describes AI credits and additional purchasable credits; no MCP-specific credit charge was found.
B_access_pricing.other_access_restrictions: Available tools depend on the approved scope. Users select an organization and scope during OAuth authorization. API-key access is also documented. No MCP-specific admin switch, client allowlist, or rate limit was found.
B_access_pricing.restrictions_controlled_by: Vendor and Close organization authorization determine available scopes; users choose the organization and scope when authorizing.

C_capabilities.description_what_how: The official reference lists tools in cumulative scopes: 75 read tools, 19 safe-write tools, and 40 destructive-scope tools. Higher scopes include lower-scope tools.
C_capabilities.post_interaction_context_structure: The official tool reference describes returned content for some tools, but does not provide a general result or error schema.

The authorization-server metadata lists authorization_endpoint https://app.close.com/oauth2/authorize/, token_endpoint https://api.close.com/oauth2/token/, registration_endpoint https://api.close.com/oauth2/register/, revocation_endpoint https://api.close.com/oauth2/revoke/, grant_types_supported ["authorization_code","refresh_token"], code_challenge_methods_supported ["S256"], response_types_supported ["code"], response_modes_supported ["query"], and token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported ["none","client_secret_basic","client_secret_post"]. D_server_side_logic.additional_logic: 1. Official tools are grouped into read-only, safe-write, and destructive scopes. Tool reference does not publish MCP annotation fields such as readOnlyHint or destructiveHint. 2. No server-enforced user-confirmation parameter or elicitation flow is documented. Tool descriptions recommend confirmation for some actions; applying a voice-agent proposal requires its proposal ID, but human approval is not technically verified in the documented interface. 3. OAuth scopes are mcp.read, mcp.write_safe, and mcp.write_destructive; higher scopes include lower ones. Docs say users grant access to an organization and scope. Product-role inheritance details, admin switches, redirect approval, and token lifetime are Unknown. OAuth metadata provides a revocation endpoint. 4. Scope controls tool availability. No read-only URL, toolset filter, query-free mode, sandbox, or regional variant found. Docs say SSE is unsupported. 5. Tools access organization CRM records; some are explicitly scoped to the current user or one lead. No general PII masking policy found. Email-thread fetch returns recent plaintext bodies and IDs for older messages. 6. Published limits include a maximum 366-day explicit range for AI credit usage and tool-specific pagination/capped report rows. General MCP rate limits, quotas, and per-call costs are Unknown. 7. No general parameter-coercion or unknown-argument policy documented. Tool descriptions specify some behavior, such as updates changing only provided fields and enrichment writing only empty fields by default. 8. Privacy policy describes operational system logs generally; MCP-specific audit records, event fields, and telemetry opt-out are Unknown. 9. No feedback/rating/survey/report tool found. `propose_voice_agent_update` accepts natural-language feedback to prepare a configuration proposal. No MCP-result upsell identified. 10. Tool descriptions steer agent behavior; the Cursor plugin also distributes a Close CRM skill outside the server. Confirmation recommendations in descriptions are not documented as enforced by the server. 11. Memory/state behavior is Unknown. `merge_leads` is asynchronous and `fetch_lead_merge` reads its status; applying a voice-agent update requires a server-stored proposal ID. 12. Flat scope-grouped tool list; voice-agent actions operate on Close features, but no nested MCP server or proxy hierarchy is documented. 13. No raw API request, SQL, script execution, or universal escape-hatch tool appears in the official list.
behavioural_instructions_to_ai_verbatim: Before the first aggregation, call `get_fields` without arguments to get the overview of every type: its fields, their value types and enum values.
Use this tool when users ask about:
If in an interactive session, ask the user for the relevant field values (including custom fields) before creating, even if they are not required.
Confirm the name and criteria with the user before creating the view.
ONLY call this if the user specifically instructed you to delete the lead, and you confirmed what the deletion will entail and that it cannot be reversed.

Before merging suspected duplicates, show the leads, why they appear to match, which lead will be kept, and any conflicting information. Ask the user to approve the specific pair or group unless they already authorized it.
Use `find_voice_agents` first to discover which voice agents are available in this organization.
Leave this tag intact or the signature could get duplicated later.
D_server_side_logic.server_structure_explanation: The official docs describe a flat tool list separated by cumulative permission scope, without documented sub-servers or dynamically loaded toolsets.

E_aggregated.action_count_comment: The official tool list exists at https://developer.close.com/mcp/tools and names 134 tools: 75 read, 19 safe-write, and 40 destructive-scope tools; the page does not state a total. All official names are in actions.json. No catalogue-only tools were added. Claude’s third-party connector directory displays a 55-tool count, so it is lower than the current official list; its list is not used in place of the official reference.

actions.description: Aggregate Close records by fields and filters.
Fetch an arbitrary supported object by ID.
Read account plan, billing, seats and AI allowance.
Fetch another page of search results.
Prepare a voice-agent change proposal without applying it.
Search leads or contacts with natural language.
Create an unsent email draft for review.
Apply a previously approved voice-agent update.
AI-enrich and write a lead or contact field.
Schedule an AI voice agent to call a contact.

E_aggregated.token_method: No public server implementation or verbatim initialize/tool-definition payload was available. The Cursor plugin repository is a client-side integration, not the deployed server code.
E_aggregated.human_can_agent_cannot: The MCP reference lists draft-email create/update tools but no send-email tool; it exposes Close CRM tasks, records, workflows, and voice-agent calls through its listed tools. The MCP reference does not document a general REST/API pass-through tool. Sources: https://developer.close.com/mcp/tools, https://developer.close.com/mcp

F_documentation.implementation_hints_not_enforced: The plugin says: “Cursor should ask before ambiguous or destructive changes.” Tool descriptions recommend user approval for specified actions, including merges and smart-view creation. The available documentation does not show those requests being enforced by the server.
F_documentation.governance_promises: The Close Help Center states: “We will never share your data with any third parties, nor use your data for any purpose.” The privacy policy describes third-party service providers, OpenAI API use for automation, operational system logs, and data retention practices. The Cursor plugin says it connects directly and “does not contain API keys, run a local process, or send Close data through an additional service.”
F_documentation.promises_to_user: The docs describe scope-based read/write/delete access and say users can revoke access. The plugin recommends choosing the least-privileged scope. Close’s general privacy policy describes retention for active accounts or as needed for the collection purpose, with deletion or anonymization afterward where applicable.
F_documentation.comparison_with_server_logic: Scope-based tool availability and OAuth revocation are documented. The specific user-confirmation recommendations are behavioral guidance, not documented server-enforced approval checks. General data-handling and logging statements are not tied to MCP-specific implementation details. The broad Help Center no-third-party-sharing statement sits alongside the privacy policy’s descriptions of third-party processors and services.

contradictions: The official tool reference lists 134 tools, while the Claude connector directory lists 55; the directory appears to be a shorter list and was not used to replace official names.

The Help Center data-security page says Close will never share data with third parties, while the privacy policy describes third-party processors and services, including OpenAI API use for automation and operational system logs. These are general Close statements, not MCP-specific implementation evidence.
observations_for_research: Tool availability is separated into three cumulative OAuth scopes, with destructive operations isolated in the highest scope.
Some write tools create drafts or proposals that require a later action to apply or send; other descriptions recommend user confirmation without documenting a server-enforced approval mechanism.
The official list includes CRM billing and AI-credit read tools as well as voice-agent management and call scheduling.
